title: Chicken Casserole with Cider and Tarragon
subtitle: Chicken thighs braised in cider with cream and tarragon
excerpt: Bone-in chicken thighs braised in dry cider with shallots, bacon, and tarragon, finished with a splash of cream. The cider reduces to a golden, slightly sweet sauce that works against the richness of the chicken.
sourceNotes: Chicken braised in cider is a dish from the apple-growing counties of England, particularly Somerset, Devon, and Herefordshire, where dry cider is the local drink. The combination of cider, cream, and tarragon is shared with French Normandy cooking but has been present in English regional cookery at least since the eighteenth century.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cream-based sauces separate when frozen. Make the base up to the point of adding cream, freeze that, and stir in cream when reheating.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The casserole can be made a day ahead without the cream and tarragon. Reheat gently, then add cream and tarragon for the last 5 minutes.

glossaryTerms.definition: Fermented apple juice with little or no residual sugar. Used in cooking, it adds a gentle acidity and apple flavour to braises and sauces. Sweet cider will make the sauce cloying; use the driest you can find.

content.text: Chicken with cider and tarragon is a one-pan braise: bone-in thighs cooked in

with shallots and bacon, finished with cream and fresh tarragon. The cider reduces to a glossy sauce with a mild, fruity edge. Use dry rather than sweet cider: sweet cider produces a sauce that is too sugary. Bone-in thighs are better than breast here; they stay moist during a longer braise.

content.text: Season the {{chicken-thigh}} of chicken thighs all over with salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a large casserole or wide saucepan over medium-high heat. Brown the chicken skin-side down for 5 to 6 minutes until golden. Turn and cook for 2 minutes on the other side. Remove and set aside.
Lower the heat to medium. Add the bacon and cook for 3 minutes until starting to brown. Add the shallots and cook for 5 minutes until golden, then add the garlic for another minute.
Pour in {{dry-cider}} of dry cider and {{stock-chicken}} of chicken stock. Return the chicken to the pan skin-side up. Bring to a simmer, then cover and cook over low heat for 30 minutes.
Uncover and cook for a further 10 minutes until the chicken is cooked through and the sauce has reduced by about a third.

Stir in the mustard and {{double-cream}} of double cream. Simmer for 3 minutes until the sauce is glossy. Remove from the heat and stir in most of the tarragon leaves. Taste and adjust seasoning. Scatter the remaining tarragon over before serving.

rows.cause: Sweet cider used instead of dry
rows.fix: Add a squeeze of lemon juice and stir in a little more mustard. Next time, use the driest cider you can find.

rows.symptom: Sauce has split and looks greasy
rows.cause: Cream added to a boiling liquid
rows.fix: Keep the heat at a gentle simmer when the cream goes in. If it splits, lower the heat immediately and stir steadily until it comes back together.

rows.symptom: Chicken skin is soft rather than crisp
rows.cause: Lid left on for the uncovered portion of cooking
rows.fix: Remove the lid for the final 10 minutes. This allows the skin to firm up in the evaporating steam.

content.text: Chicken braised in cider comes from the apple-growing counties of south-west England, where dry farmhouse cider was the default cooking liquid in the same way wine is used in French braises. The combination with cream and tarragon connects the dish to Normandy cooking across the Channel, but the English version is less refined and more rustic. It is the kind of supper that works on a weeknight but is good enough for a small dinner party.
